query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: An enhanced free energy calculation framework that integrates machine-learned interatomic potentials with advanced sampling techniques (e.g., metadynamics or nested sampling) can accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the compositional space of high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys in their as-cast or thermally processed solid-state configuration, exhibiting complex multicomponent disorder.
generation.intervention: Implement a simulation protocol that uses state-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic potentials combined with advanced free energy sampling algorithms to trace the entire solid–liquid coexistence region.
generation.conditions: High-temperature melting conditions under near-equilibrium (or controlled non-equilibrium) scenarios applicable to HEAs with ≥5 principal elements; requires that the ML potentials are pre-trained and validated on relevant HEA configurations.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolving solid–liquid interface and the free energy landscape that governs the phase coexistence during melting, capturing both local atomic rearrangements and overall latent heat signatures.
generation.mechanism: The approach leverages machine-learned potentials to accurately capture complex interatomic interactions and uses advanced sampling methods to efficiently explore the rugged free energy landscape. This allows precise determination of thermodynamic quantities such as latent heat (from the computed free energy differences) and volume changes at melting by following the phase boundary evolution.
generation.predicted_outcome: The framework is expected to predict melting points, latent heats, and volume changes within an error margin that is competitive with high-fidelity calorimetric measurements while achieving higher throughput. A consistent reproduction of sharp phase coexistence and latent heat signatures across varying HEA compositions is anticipated.
generation.baseline: Conventional differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and traditional molecular dynamics approaches with standard interatomic potentials, which are less efficient and may not capture the full configurational complexity of HEAs.
generation.boundary: The approach depends on the transferability and accuracy of the machine-learned potentials; it may be less applicable to alloys whose compositions or local structural effects are poorly represented in the training set. Extremely complex HEAs outside the training range may exhibit deviations.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement (e.g., accuracy better by an estimated 10-20% over traditional methods) is uncertain and will depend on the quality of the ML potentials and the efficiency of the sampling strategy.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of high-throughput simulations on a range of HEA compositions using the enhanced framework and compare the simulated melting temperature, latent heat (fusion enthalpy and entropy), and volume change at melting with high-precision DSC and X-ray/neutron scattering measurements. The simulations should cover both well-characterized and less-common compositions.
measurements: Fusion enthalpy and entropy from calorimetric measurements
Volume change at melting via in situ X-ray or neutron scattering
Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties via complementary calorimetry and high-temperature property measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulation predictions consistently deviate from experimental values by more than the accepted experimental error margin (e.g., ±10%) across multiple compositions, thereby failing to reproduce the sharp phase coexistence and latent heat signatures, the validity of the enhanced free energy framework would be refuted.

cited_evidence.text:
The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. In the example of the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system, it takes only a few hours on a desktop computer to finish the HTCs (~ 3 × 10 3 ) within the composition range of 5–50 at.% for each element and finally screen out eight potential alloys. The CALPHAD-based HTCs

The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. decision.trend: Historically, researchers attempted to characterize high‐entropy alloys at high temperatures using calorimetric experiments (e.g., DSC) and equilibrium phase diagram construction, while early computational approaches (molecular dynamics and thermodynamic integration) were explored but had to compromise on configurational complexity and efficiency. More recently, high‐throughput computational screening and multiscale modelling (as seen in PMC8282813 and PMC10213035) have been used to target high-temperature performance properties, yet these studies focused on solid-state and mechanical properties rather than a detailed mapping of fusion thermodynamics. This reflects an evolution from direct experimental probing to advanced computational methods, though none have yet fully addressed the challenges of accurately capturing the liquid-phase thermodynamic properties and phase transition details in the vast compositional space of HEAs.
decision.unsolved: The primary unsolved challenge is how to reliably and efficiently compute the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change on melting, and other liquid-phase properties for high-entropy alloys despite their intrinsic multicomponent disorder. Neither traditional calorimetry nor conventional simulation has provided a physically transparent, sufficiently accurate, and high-throughput method across the entire compositional space.
decision.lever: Develop an enhanced free energy calculation framework that integrates state-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic potentials with advanced sampling techniques (e.g., metadynamics or nested sampling) to accurately trace the solid–liquid coexistence and compute fusion thermodynamics.
decision.why: This approach builds naturally on the trend from conventional calorimetry and approximated molecular dynamics to high-throughput, physically motivated simulation methods. By leveraging advanced sampling strategies in combination with machine-learning potentials, the method promises both the quantitative accuracy and efficiency required for covering a broad range of HEA compositions, and its decisive validation would come from reproducing sharp phase coexistence and latent heat signatures that rule out oversimplified modeling.
